intro: Look around you. A book is a rectangle. A clock is a circle. A ball is a sphere. Shapes are in every room and on every street. In this unit you learn to name them. You count sides and corners. You find solids that roll and solids that stack.

Then you learn to cut shapes into equal parts. Two kids share a sandwich. Four kids share a pizza. Each one wants a fair share. You will cut halves, thirds and fourths. You will see that a fair share is an equal share.
By the end you can name a shape by its sides. You can build a big shape from small ones. You can cut a whole into equal parts and name each part. That is a lot of power for a pair of scissors.
bigQuestion: How do we name a shape, and how do we cut it so every share is fair?

timeline.t: Look at a flat shape. Is it round or does it have straight sides?
Count the sides. Three, four or six?
Count the corners. Every straight side meets another at a corner.
Say the name: triangle, square, rectangle, hexagon or circle.
Pick up a solid. Does it roll, stack or both?
Name the solid: cube, sphere, cone or cylinder.
Join small shapes to build a bigger one.
Fold a shape in half. Check that the two parts match.
Cut thirds and fourths. Count the equal parts.
Share with friends. Give everyone an equal part.

words.d: one straight edge of a flat shape
the point where two sides of a shape meet
a flat shape with six straight sides and six corners
a solid shape with 6 flat square faces, like a dice
a solid shape with two flat circle ends and a curved side, like a can
one of two equal parts of a whole
one of four equal parts of a whole, also called a quarter
a line of squares that goes across, from left to right

test.q: How many sides does a square have?
test.why: A square has four equal straight sides and four square corners.

test.q: Which flat shape has six sides?
test.why: A hexagon has six sides and six corners. A triangle has three and a rectangle has four.

test.q: Which solid shape has no flat faces?
test.why: A sphere is round all over with no flat face. A cube has 6 and a cylinder has 2.

test.q: A can of soup is what solid shape?
test.why: A can has a circle on top, a circle on the bottom and a curved side. That is a cylinder.

test.q: Two same-size squares placed side by side make what shape?
test.why: Two squares in a row make a shape with two long sides and two short sides. That is a rectangle.

test.q: A pizza is cut into four equal slices. Each slice is what?
test.why: Four equal parts of a whole are fourths. Each slice is one fourth, or one quarter.

test.q: How many thirds make one whole?
test.why: Three equal parts put together make the whole. So 3 thirds make one whole.

test.q: A square is cut into one big piece and one small piece. Are the pieces halves?
choices: Yes, if the square is small
test.why: Halves are two equal parts. A big piece and a small piece are not equal.

test.q: A bar has 3 rows of 2 squares. How many squares in all?
test.why: Add the rows: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 squares. Adding 3 + 2 = 5 is the common mistake.

test.q: Which is bigger, one half of a cookie or one fourth of the same cookie?
test.why: Two parts are bigger than four parts of the same whole. So one half is bigger than one fourth.

write.prompt: Three friends want to share one square brownie fairly. Draw how you would cut it. Then tell what each friend gets and how you know the shares are equal.
tips: Say how many equal pieces you need and why.
Tell how many cuts you make.
Say how you would check that the pieces are the same size.

title: Shapes and Equal Shares

chapters.title: Flat and Solid Shapes
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we know a shape is a triangle, no matter how big it is or how it turns?

story.title: The Block City
story.kicker: A class builds a city out of blocks and starts to see shapes everywhere.
paragraphs: On Friday the blocks came out. Mia and Jon built a tall tower. Ava built a bridge. Sam made a road with long flat blocks. Soon the rug was a whole city. It had houses, a school and a park.

Then Ms. Lee asked a question. "What shapes do you see?" Mia looked at the side of her tower. "A square!" she said. Jon looked at the roof. "A triangle. It has three sides." Ava found a circle on the end of a round block.
Sam held up a block. It looked like a can of soup. "What is this one?" No one knew the name. Ms. Lee smiled. "That is a cylinder. It rolls and it stacks." Sam rolled it down the road.
The class walked around the city. They found squares, rectangles, triangles and circles. They found cubes, cones and spheres. Shapes were hiding in every block. They just had to look.
story.think: Look around your room right now. What is one shape you can see, and how do you know its name?

lessons.title: Sides and Corners
lessons.mainIdea: We name a flat shape by counting its sides and corners.
reading: Look at a slice of pizza. It has three straight edges. A shape with three straight *sides* is a *triangle*. Where two sides meet, there is a *corner*. A triangle has three corners too.
Now look at a cracker. It has four sides. All four are the same length. All four corners are square, like the corner of a book. That shape is a square.
A door has four sides too. But two sides are long and two are short. That shape is a rectangle. To name a shape, count the sides. Then look at the corners.

words.d: one straight edge of a flat shape
the point where two sides of a shape meet
a flat shape with three straight sides and three corners

look.title: Count the Sides
look.text: Picture a yield sign on the road. It has three straight sides. Now picture a stop sign next to it. Count its sides in your head. It has eight. A stop sign is not a triangle. It is a shape called an octagon.
look.prompt: How many corners does the yield sign have? How do you know without counting them?

check.q: A shape has three straight sides. What is it?
check.why: Three straight sides make a triangle. A square has four sides. A circle has no straight sides.

check.q: How many corners does a square have?
check.why: A square has four sides, and each pair of sides meets at a corner. That makes 4 corners.

check.q: A shape has four sides. Two are long and two are short. What is it?
check.why: Four sides with two long and two short make a rectangle. A triangle has three sides. A circle has none.

lessons.title: Hexagons and Circles
lessons.mainIdea: A hexagon has six sides; a circle is round with no sides at all.
reading: Look at a honeycomb. Each little room has six sides. A shape with six straight sides is a *hexagon*. It has six corners too. Count them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Now look at a clock face or a coin. It is round. It has no straight sides. It has no corners. That shape is a *circle*. Every spot on the edge is the same distance from the middle.
Here is a common mistake. Some kids think a big triangle is a different shape than a small one. It is not. Size does not change the name. Only the sides and corners do.

words.d: a flat shape with six straight sides and six corners
a round flat shape with no straight sides and no corners

look.title: Sides on Each Shape
look.cite: standard counts of straight sides for each flat shape
look.prompt: Which two shapes have the same number of sides? How can you tell them apart?

check.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
check.why: A hexagon has six sides and six corners, like one room in a honeycomb.

check.q: Which shape has no corners?
check.why: A circle is round with no straight sides, so it has no corners. Triangles have 3 and hexagons have 6.

check.q: A tiny triangle and a huge triangle. Are they the same shape?
choices: No, the big one is a square
check.why: Both have three straight sides and three corners. Size does not change a shape's name.

lessons.title: Cubes and Spheres
lessons.mainIdea: Solid shapes take up space; a cube has flat square faces and a sphere is round all over.
reading: A drawing of a square is flat. A dice is not flat. You can hold it. It is a *solid* shape. Solid shapes take up space. A dice is a *cube*. Every face is a square.
Count the faces on a dice. Top, bottom, front, back, left, right. That is 6 faces. A cube has 6 square faces. It stacks well because the faces are flat.
A ball is a solid shape too. It is round all over. It has no flat faces and no corners. That shape is a *sphere*. A sphere rolls any way you push it.

words.d: a shape that takes up space, not flat, like a block or a ball
a solid shape with 6 flat square faces, like a dice
a solid shape that is round all over, like a ball

look.title: Roll or Stack?
look.text: Picture a cube and a sphere on a table. Push the cube. It slides and stops. Push the sphere. It rolls away. Now try to put a cube on top of another cube. It stays. Try to put a sphere on top of a sphere. It falls off.
look.prompt: Why does a cube stack but a sphere does not? What part of each shape makes the difference?

check.q: How many faces does a cube have?
check.why: A cube has 6 faces: top, bottom, front, back, left and right. Each face is a square.

check.q: Which solid shape is round all over?
check.why: A sphere is round all over, like a ball. A cube has flat faces. A square is flat, not solid.

check.q: What shape is each face of a cube?
check.why: Every face of a cube is a square with four equal sides. That is what makes it a cube.

lessons.title: Cones and Cylinders
lessons.mainIdea: A cylinder has two flat circle faces; a cone has one circle face and a point.
reading: Look at a can of soup. The top is a circle. The bottom is a circle. The side is curved. That solid shape is a *cylinder*. A cylinder stacks on its flat end. It rolls on its side.
Now look at a party hat or an ice cream cone. The bottom is a circle. The top comes to a point. That shape is a *cone*. A cone stands on its circle. It cannot stack on its point.
Some kids mix up a cylinder and a cone. Check the ends. Two circles means a cylinder. One circle and a point means a cone.

words.d: a solid shape with two flat circle ends and a curved side, like a can
a solid shape with one flat circle and a point, like a party hat

look.title: Flat Faces on Solids
look.cite: standard counts of flat faces on each solid shape
look.prompt: Which solid has the most flat faces? Which has none? Which one could you not stand a cup on?

check.q: Which solid shape has two flat circle ends?
check.why: A cylinder has a circle on top and a circle on the bottom, like a can. A cone has only one.

check.q: A party hat has one circle and a point. What shape is it?
check.why: One flat circle plus a point on top makes a cone. A sphere has no flat face. A cylinder has two.

check.q: How many flat faces does a cone have?
check.why: A cone has just 1 flat face, the circle it stands on. The rest is curved and ends at a point.

lessons.title: Putting Shapes Together
lessons.mainIdea: Small shapes can join to make a bigger shape.
reading: Take two squares that are the same size. Put them side by side. Now you have one long shape. It has four sides. Two are long and two are short. Two squares make a rectangle.
Take a square and cut it from corner to corner. You get two triangles. Put them back together. The square is back. Shapes can split apart and *join* up again.
Try this with six triangles. Put their points in the middle. They make a hexagon. Building shapes from shapes is how blocks make a city.

words.d: to put two or more shapes together to make a new shape

look.title: Two Triangles
look.text: Picture two triangles that are the same size. Each one looks like half a square. Put the two long sides together. What do you see? Now turn one of them around. Put the short sides together. You get a different shape. Same two pieces, two different results.
look.prompt: What shape do two of these triangles make when the long sides touch? What new shape could you make with four of them?

check.q: Two same-size squares side by side make what shape?
check.why: Two squares in a row make a shape with two long sides and two short sides. That is a rectangle.

check.q: Cut a square from corner to corner. What do you get?
check.why: The cut makes two shapes with three sides each. Each one is a triangle.

check.q: Six triangles with points in the middle make what shape?
check.why: The six outside edges become six sides. Six sides make a hexagon.

lessons.title: Drawing a Shape
lessons.mainIdea: To draw a shape, decide the number of sides and corners first.
reading: Ms. Lee says, "Draw a shape with four sides." You could draw a square. You could draw a rectangle. Both have four sides. Both are right. The *rule* tells you what counts.
Now she says, "Draw a shape with three corners." That is a triangle. It can be tall or short. It can point up or sideways. It is still a triangle if it has three sides and three corners.
Here is a trap. A shape with four sides but one side bent is not a square. Sides must be straight. Check each side with a ruler if you are not sure.

words.d: what a shape must have, like four sides or three corners

look.title: Follow the Rule
look.text: Jon drew a shape with four straight sides. All the sides are the same length. All the corners are square. Ava drew a shape with four straight sides too. Two sides are longer than the others. Both followed the rule "four sides." But they drew different shapes.
look.prompt: What did Jon draw? What did Ava draw? Could both drawings be right?

check.q: The rule is "three sides." Which shape fits?
check.why: A triangle has three sides. A square has four and a hexagon has six.

check.q: Which shape fits the rule "four sides"?
check.why: A rectangle has four straight sides. A circle has none. A triangle has three.

check.q: A shape has four sides, but one side is curved. Is it a square?
choices: No, the sides must be straight
check.why: A square needs four straight sides. A curved side breaks the rule, so it is not a square.

lessons.title: Shapes Around Us
lessons.mainIdea: Shapes are everywhere: in signs, buildings and floors.
reading: Walk down a street in Chicago. A stop sign has eight sides. A window is a rectangle. A manhole cover is a circle. Shapes are on every block.
Look at a floor made of *tiles*. The tiles are often squares. They fit with no gaps. Squares fit together well because their corners are square. Hexagon tiles fit too.
Look up at a tall building. Its sides are rectangles. A roof may be a triangle. Now find a solid. A trash can is a cylinder. A ball in the park is a sphere.

words.d: a flat shape used to cover a floor or wall with no gaps

look.title: A Walk to School
look.text: Picture your walk to school. You pass a red stop sign with eight sides. You pass a house with a door. The door has four sides. The roof comes to a point with three sides. At school the clock on the wall is round. The tiles on the floor are squares.
look.prompt: Name the shape of the door, the roof and the clock. Which solid shape is a trash can?

check.q: A window with four sides, two long and two short, is what shape?
check.why: Four sides with two long and two short make a rectangle.

check.q: A trash can with a round top and bottom is what solid?
check.why: A round top, a round bottom and a curved side make a cylinder, like a can.

check.q: Why do square tiles cover a floor with no gaps?
choices: Their corners are square and fit together
check.why: Four square corners meet at a point and fill the space, so square tiles leave no gaps.

review.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
review.why: A triangle has three straight sides and three corners.
A hexagon has six sides. Squares and rectangles have four.

review.q: Which solid shape is like a ball?
review.why: A sphere is round all over, like a ball. A cube has flat faces and a cylinder has two circle ends.

review.q: How many square faces does a cube have?
review.why: A cube has 6 faces, and each face is a square.

review.q: A big square and a small square. Are they the same shape?
choices: Yes, size does not change the name
No, the small one is a triangle
No, the big one is a rectangle
review.why: Both have four equal straight sides and four square corners. Size does not change the name.

review.q: Two same-size squares side by side make what?
review.why: Two squares in a row make a shape with two long sides and two short sides. That is a rectangle.

chapters.title: Halves, Thirds and Fourths
chapters.bigQuestion: What makes a share fair, and how can we cut a shape so every share is the same?

story.title: One Sandwich, Two Kids
story.kicker: Two hungry kids, one sandwich, and a fight over the word fair.
paragraphs: Ben and Rosa got home from school. They were hungry. There was one sandwich on the plate. Ben grabbed a knife. He cut the sandwich. One piece was big. One piece was small. Ben took the big one.
"That is not fair!" said Rosa. "Your piece is bigger." Ben looked at the two pieces. He knew she was right. Two pieces is not the same as two equal pieces. Fair means the same size.
Their dad came in. He put the pieces back together. "Let's try again," he said. He cut the sandwich down the middle. Now both pieces were the same. "Each of you gets one half," he said.
Rosa held up her piece. "Half," she said. Ben held up his. "Half." Two halves. One whole sandwich. Both kids were happy. And both learned a new word for fair.
story.think: Ben cut the sandwich into two pieces. Why was that still not fair? What did the second cut do differently?

lessons.title: What Half Means
lessons.mainIdea: A half is one of two equal parts of a whole.
reading: Take a paper circle. Fold it so the edges match. Open it up. The fold cuts the circle into two parts. The two parts are the same size. They are *equal*. Each part is one *half*.
Now take a paper square. Cut it into two parts. But make one part big and one part small. Are those halves? No. Halves must be equal. Two unequal pieces are not halves.
Two halves make one whole. Put the two halves of the circle back together. The whole circle is back. Say it like this: one half and one half make one whole.

words.d: the same size or the same amount
one of two equal parts of a whole
the full thing before it is cut into parts

look.title: Fold and Check
look.text: Picture a square piece of paper. Fold it so the top edge lands right on the bottom edge. Press the fold. Open it. You see two parts. Put one part on top of the other in your mind. They match. That is how you know they are equal.
look.prompt: What is each part called? If you fold the paper the other way, from left to right, are the parts still halves?

check.q: A circle is cut into two equal parts. What is each part called?
check.why: Two equal parts of a whole are halves. Each part is one half.

check.q: A square is cut into one big piece and one small piece. Are they halves?
choices: Yes, if the square is big
check.why: Halves are two equal parts. A big piece and a small piece are not equal, so they are not halves.

check.q: How many halves make one whole?
check.why: One half and one half make one whole. That is 2 halves.

lessons.title: Halves Can Look Different
lessons.mainIdea: Two halves of the same whole are equal even if they are different shapes.
reading: Take two paper squares the same size. Cut the first one straight down the middle. You get two tall rectangles. Each one is a half.

Cut the second square from corner to corner. You get two triangles. Each one is a half too. A rectangle half and a triangle half look different. But they came from the same square. They are the same size.
Here is the rule. Halves of the same whole are always equal in size. Their shape can be different. Kids often think the triangle half is smaller. Check by cutting. It is not.

words.d: the outline of a part, like a triangle or a rectangle

look.title: Two Ways to Cut
look.text: Picture a square brownie. Mia cuts hers straight across. Her two halves are rectangles. Jon cuts his from corner to corner. His two halves are triangles. Both brownies were the same size to start. Mia takes one of her halves. Jon takes one of his.
look.prompt: Who has more brownie, Mia or Jon? How do you know?

check.q: A square cut corner to corner makes two halves. What shape are they?
check.why: A corner-to-corner cut makes two pieces with three sides each. They are triangles.

check.q: A rectangle half and a triangle half come from the same square. Which is bigger?
check.why: Both are one half of the same square, so they are the same size even though they look different.

check.q: Can two halves of one whole be different shapes?
choices: Yes, if they are the same size
check.why: Halves must be equal in size, not in shape. A square can be halved into rectangles or into triangles.

lessons.title: Thirds
lessons.mainIdea: A third is one of three equal parts of a whole.
reading: Three friends share one granola bar. They cut it into three equal pieces. Each piece is one *third*. Each friend gets one third of the bar.
To cut a rectangle into thirds, make two cuts. Not three. Two cuts make three pieces. Make the pieces the same size. Check by laying one piece on another.
Three thirds make one whole. Put the three pieces back. The bar is whole again. A common mistake is to make three cuts. That gives four pieces, not three.

words.d: one of three equal parts of a whole

look.title: Cuts and Pieces
look.cite: cutting a bar straight across, one cut at a time
look.prompt: How many cuts make thirds? How many cuts would you need for five equal pieces?

check.q: A bar is cut into three equal parts. What is each part called?
check.why: Three equal parts of a whole are thirds. Each part is one third.

check.q: How many cuts across a bar make three pieces?
check.why: Each cut adds one piece. Start with 1 piece. Two cuts make 1 + 2 = 3 pieces.

check.q: How many thirds make one whole?
check.why: One third plus one third plus one third makes one whole. That is 3 thirds.

lessons.title: Fourths and Quarters
lessons.mainIdea: A fourth, also called a quarter, is one of four equal parts.
reading: Four kids share a small pizza. They cut it into four equal slices. Each slice is one *fourth*. Another name for one fourth is one *quarter*. Both words mean the same thing.
To cut a square into fourths, fold it in half. Then fold it in half again. Open it. You see four equal squares. Four fourths make one whole.
Fourths are smaller than halves. Think about the pizza. Cut it in half, and you get a big slice. Cut it in fourths, and you get a smaller slice. More parts means smaller parts.

words.d: one of four equal parts of a whole
another name for one fourth, like a quarter coin is one fourth of a dollar

look.title: Slices in One Pizza
look.cite: one whole pizza cut into equal slices
look.prompt: Which cut gives the smallest slice? Which cut gives the biggest? Why?

check.q: What is another name for one fourth?
check.why: One fourth and one quarter both mean one of four equal parts.

check.q: How many fourths make one whole?
check.why: Four equal parts put together make the whole. So 4 fourths make one whole.

check.q: Which is smaller, one half of a pizza or one fourth of the same pizza?
check.why: Cutting into more parts makes smaller parts. Four parts are smaller than two, so one fourth is smaller.

lessons.title: Squares in Rows and Columns
lessons.mainIdea: A rectangle can be cut into rows and columns of same-size squares.
reading: Look at a chocolate bar. It is made of small squares. The squares go across in *rows*. They go up and down in *columns*. Count the rows: 2. Count the squares in each row: 3.
Now count all the squares. Row one has 3. Row two has 3. That is 3 + 3 = 6 squares. You can also add the columns: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. Same answer.
Try a bigger bar. It has 3 rows. Each row has 4 squares. Add: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The bar has 12 squares. Counting by rows is faster than counting one by one.

words.d: a line of squares that goes across, from left to right
a line of squares that goes up and down

look.title: Squares in a Bar
look.cite: a chocolate bar with 4 squares in each row
look.prompt: What pattern do you see as you add a row? How many squares would 5 rows of 4 have?

check.q: A bar has 2 rows. Each row has 3 squares. How many squares in all?
check.why: Add the rows: 3 + 3 = 6 squares. Adding 2 + 3 = 5 is a mistake, since that mixes rows and squares.

check.q: A bar has 3 rows of 4 squares. How many squares in all?
check.why: Add 4 three times: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Adding 3 + 4 = 7 is the common mistake.

check.q: A line of squares going across a bar is called what?
check.why: A row goes across, left to right. A column goes up and down.

lessons.title: Sharing Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: A fair share means every person gets an equal part of the whole.
reading: Two kids share one pancake. Cut it into halves. Each kid gets one half. Three kids share one pancake. Cut it into thirds. Each kid gets one third.
Four kids share one pancake. Cut it into fourths. Each kid gets one fourth. Count the people. Cut that many equal parts. That is a *fair share*.
Watch out for this mistake. Ben cut a pancake into two big pieces and one small one for three kids. Three pieces, but not equal. That is not thirds. Not fair.

words.d: a part that is the same size as everyone else's part

look.title: The Birthday Cake
look.text: Picture a square birthday cake. Four cousins want cake. Their aunt cuts it once down the middle. Then she cuts it once across the middle. Now there are four equal squares. Each cousin gets one. Then a fifth cousin walks in. Everyone looks at the cake.
look.prompt: What is each cousin's share called? What could the aunt have done if she knew five cousins were coming?

check.q: Three kids share one pancake fairly. What does each kid get?
check.why: Three people means three equal parts. Each part is one third.

check.q: Four kids share one cake. How many equal pieces should it have?
check.why: One piece for each of the 4 kids. So the cake needs 4 equal pieces, or fourths.

check.q: A pancake is cut into three pieces. Two are big and one is small. Is that fair for three kids?
choices: No, the pieces are not equal
Yes, if the pancake is round
check.why: Fair shares must be equal. Three pieces of different sizes are not thirds, so it is not fair.

review.q: A sandwich is cut into two equal parts. Each part is called what?
review.why: Two equal parts of a whole are halves.

review.q: How many fourths make one whole?
review.why: Four equal parts make the whole. So 4 fourths make one whole.

review.q: A square is cut into two rectangles. Another same-size square is cut into two triangles. Which half is bigger?
review.why: Both are one half of the same-size square, so they are the same size even though they look different.

review.q: A bar has 2 rows of 5 squares. How many squares in all?
review.why: Add the rows: 5 + 5 = 10 squares. Adding 2 + 5 = 7 is a mistake.

review.q: Another name for one fourth is what?
review.why: One fourth and one quarter mean the same thing: one of four equal parts.

review.q: Three friends share one bar fairly. How many equal pieces do they cut?
review.why: One equal piece for each of 3 friends means 3 pieces, or thirds.
